Systemic inflammation

Summary of the Evidence

Two publications directly examine systemic cytokine responses: a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled human experiment using broad-spectrum polarized light and a mouse surgical-inflammation experiment using near-infrared laser. A third, narrowly mapped controlled study measured serum IL-6 after local gingival PBM in people with periodontitis and type 2 diabetes. Direct irradiation of blood samples was part of the same human experiment, not an independent cohort (Zhevago and Samoilova 2006; Fukuda et al. 2013; Mrasori et al. 2021).

Human and clinical evidence

In a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind experiment involving 62 volunteers, polarized visible and infrared light was applied over the sacral area. Among participants whose starting concentrations were above the reference range, TNF-α, IL-6, and IFN-γ fell by averages of 34-fold, 12-fold, and 1.5-fold at 30 minutes. TNF-α and IL-6 remained lower after four daily exposures. Other responses depended on the marker and starting level: IL-10 and TGF-β1 increased in selected subgroups, IFN-γ increased when baseline values were normal, and several cytokines did not change. These are short-term laboratory outcomes rather than evidence of symptom relief or reduced disease activity (Zhevago and Samoilova 2006).

The mapped periodontal study enrolled 80 people with periodontitis and type 2 diabetes. Adding local 660-nm gingival PBM to conservative periodontal treatment was associated with lower serum IL-6 at six weeks and three months. Because treatment was applied to the gingiva in a specific dental population, this is related evidence about a systemic biomarker response rather than a trial of systemic PBM (Mrasori et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

In a 50-mouse surgical-inflammation experiment, 780-nm near-infrared laser decreased TNF-α and IFN-γ release from spleen mononuclear cells, particularly after two sessions. IL-6 and TGF-β1 did not change, showing that the response was marker-specific (Fukuda et al. 2013).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The randomized human publication also irradiated blood samples from the same volunteers directly at 2.4 J/cm². Some cytokine patterns resembled those seen after transcutaneous exposure, but this component does not add an independent human treatment cohort (Zhevago and Samoilova 2006).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human experiment used 480–3400-nm polarized light at 12 J/cm² over the sacral area and 2.4 J/cm² for blood samples, with five daily 300-second exposures. This broad spectrum extends beyond conventional red and near-infrared PBM. The mouse experiment used 780 nm at 10 J/cm² and 20 mW at three points, with one to three sessions. The mapped periodontal study used local 660-nm light over five days. These protocols and anatomical targets are not interchangeable (Zhevago and Samoilova 2006; Fukuda et al. 2013; Mrasori et al. 2021).

Interpretation

Selected cytokines can change after light exposure, but the direction depends on the marker, baseline concentration, protocol, and treatment site. The available studies do not show that these laboratory changes reduce symptoms, complications, or inflammatory-disease activity.

Publications and records

3 relevant publications

Two direct systemic-inflammation studies and one narrow periodontal mapping.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for short-term changes in selected blood cytokines after broad-spectrum polarized light exposure

One randomized sham-controlled experiment reported large but baseline-dependent biomarker changes and has not been independently replicated (Zhevago and Samoilova 2006).

Very low for clinical improvement in inflammatory disease

The studies measured cytokines rather than symptoms or disease activity.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One randomized sham-controlled study found large, baseline-dependent short-term changes in several cytokines after broad-spectrum 480–3400-nm polarized light, but it did not test symptoms or disease activity and has not been independently replicated. A mouse surgical-inflammation experiment found marker-specific changes, while a related periodontal study used local gingival PBM. Confidence is low for biomarker effects and very low for clinical benefit (Zhevago and Samoilova 2006; Fukuda et al. 2013; Mrasori et al. 2021).
